applies_to: revision 1.204 (baseline 1.203); edges and sources for the edge review of the 1.201 person entries Wheeler, Macdougall, Innes and McCallum (Agent A)

proposed_edges.relationship: With Denise Henning (2021), Wheeler adopts Wolfe's definition: in the Americas 'classic colonialism evolved into settler colonialism', whose goal 'is the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands and resources (Wolfe, 2006)'.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Henning and Wheeler, New Directions for Student Services 2020, nos. 171–172 (online 30 April 2021), section 'Colonization and intergenerational trauma' (early-view p. 3; print pp. 57–67); Wolfe 2006 (Journal of Genocide Research 8:4) in the references. A co-authored study (Henning first author) of rural Indigenous students' postsecondary experience: it uses the frame as historical context and does not discuss settler colonial studies as a field. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000, 2010), without settler-colonial vocabulary.

proposed_edges.relationship: Postcolonial studies as an internal challenge to conventional history that opens space for Indigenous history: Wheeler draws on Fanon and Memmi to name 'intellectual colonialism', the colonization of Indigenous histories (2000), and counts 'critical and post-/anti-colonial scholars' among her teachers (2010).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (PhD, UC Berkeley, 2000), p. 79 ('The imposition of eurocentric categories on Indigenous knowledge of the past amounts to intellectual colonialism'), p. 80 (Fanon quoted on colonialism's distortion of the past), pp. 117–118 (section 'Postcolonial Studies': Fanon and Memmi, with examples 'relevant to issues of Indigenous history … to demonstrate the value of postcolonial studies'); pages read through OCR. Wheeler 2010, p. 48.

proposed_edges.relationship: Native Studies does not belong under Ethnic Studies: to 'classify us as just another ethnic minority, it is colonialist'; 'we are not an ethnic minority … We are Indigenous', and 'Fourth World Studies is the next logical step' for comparison (1998; first given at UBC in 1995).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998): p. 33 (Native Studies 'does not belong under the rubric of Ethnic Studies'), p. 36 (Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins on lumping minority groups together), pp. 34–38 (Blauner's colonial model, whose conclusion she accepts while criticising his evidence), p. 40 ('colonialist'), p. 49 (conclusion). First presented at UBC, 2 November 1995 (p. 50 note). Protocol passages (pp. 38–39) are not used (OCAP).

proposed_edges.relationship: Outside definitions misread Indigenous oral history: Vansina's process-and-product definition of oral tradition 'does not take into account that Indigenous Peoples' have their own respective intellectual histories' (1998); recorded oral histories are not documents, and treating transcripts as written records, as William Moss proposed, strips their cultural and linguistic context (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Saskatchewan History 50:2 (Fall 1998), p. 26 (re-read 2026-10-28 by OCR of the iPortal issue PDF). Wheeler, Shekon Neechie, 20 June 2018 (community-controlled: paraphrased, not reproduced): ¶1 (oral histories are not books and should not be treated as written records), ¶2 (against Moss's view of a taped interview as a document), ¶6 (what translation and transcription lose), ¶13 (scholars must learn to read recorded narratives in their own contexts). No Elder's words, teachings or story content are used (OCAP).

proposed_edges.relationship: Wheeler takes Smith's account of colonialism's negation of Indigenous views of history (2000) and her call for intellectual decolonization through Indigenous-framed research methods (2001).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (2000), p. 80 (block quotation of Smith 1999 on the 'negation of Indigenous views of history'; OCR). Wheeler, CJNS 21:1 (2001), p. 100: Smith 'and other like-minded Indigenous scholars promote anti-colonial research and argue for intellectual decolonization through the development of Indigenous-framed research methods and approaches (see Smith, 1999)'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wheeler opens her case that Indigenous peoples are not an ethnic minority with Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) on liberals who 'categorize them all together' as minority groups, and returns to him on cooperative movements (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998), p. 36 (Deloria quoted, notes 6–9) and pp. 46–47 (Deloria 1969 on cooperative movements).

proposed_edges.relationship: Against the Supreme Court's 'mixedness' in Daniels (2016): '"mixed blood" does not equal Métis any more than "full blood" equals Indian. Both statements are based on racialized historical fictions'; the claim that the first Métis was born nine months after contact 'supports a colonial fantasy of benevolent relations'.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Macdougall, International Indigenous Policy Journal 7:3 (2016), read in full: p. 2 (the Indian Act's 'legal fiction … that cannot now distinguish Indigenous cultural identities from colonial machinations'), p. 4 (the two quotations; the Métis as a nation formed in the fur trade, centred on kinship across a historic homeland), p. 5 (Métis and Non-Status Indians: 'we must be careful not to conflate national identities'). She cites Andersen 2016 (p. 1).

proposed_edges.relationship: Historians, McCallum argues, 'have created a false dichotomy between the colonial and modern period as two distinct projects'; for Indigenous women, 1940–80, colonialism continued as the state dictated schooling, employment and labour (2014, as summarised by Patricia Harms).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Harms, review, Manitoba History 80 (Spring 2016), para. 2, read in full: 'Believing its destructive impact is in the past, historians, McCallum argues, have created a false dichotomy between the colonial and modern period as two distinct projects'; 'colonialism continued for Aboriginal women, as the state dictated education options, determined places of employment, and attempted to control women's labour practices'. Williams (BC Studies 191, 2016, read in full): her conclusion 'proposes a critical revision of historiographical methods and pedagogy in Indigenous and Canadian history'. McCallum's own text is unread; the edge rests on two named readers.

row.context: Cree historian of oral tradition and Indigenous Studies. With Denise Henning (2021) she adopts Wolfe's definition of settler colonialism ('the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands') in a study of rural Indigenous students. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000–2010).
